extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, peer reviewers, researchers studying peer review, and academic policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluate and improve the academic journal peer-review process, including reviewer behavior (bias, reliability, accountability) and editorial policies (blind review, training, open commentary). Applicable to empirical studies of peer review and recommendations for editorial practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer evaluation: Fairness, carefulness, constructiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Three dimensions proposed for author evaluation of reviews: 'Fairness, carefulness, and constructiveness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a postcard questionnaire sent with decision letters asking authors to rate each review on these three dimensions and provide comments. Editors would file returned cards under reviewers' names and periodically examine them; repeated complaints could lead to admonishment or termination of a reviewer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Response bias (criterion or cutoff bias)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers may set different acceptance cutoffs (criterion c) based on author/institutional prestige, causing systematic shifts in false-positive vs false-negative rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framed in signal-detection terms: the cutoff point for publication acceptability may be lowered or raised as a function of status variables. This bias could in principle be a valid predictor of quality and should be empirically tested (e.g., via resubmission experiments) to see whether it maximizes hits-to-misses for a journal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer reliability / interrater agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the consistency of reviewers' judgments (interreferee agreement), noting that some studies report high agreement especially in nonblind journals and for outright rejection decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure reliability statistically (e.g., chi-square tests, interrater reliability indices). Recognize that rejection decisions may show higher rater reliability (Cicchetti 1980). Consider how review format (blind vs nonblind) relates to reported interrater agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer recognition of previously published work
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether reviewers recognize resubmitted or previously published articles: in the study almost 90% of reviewers failed to recognize the resubmissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider causes (forgotten due to intervening reports; reviewers never saw or heard of the originals). Failure to recognize prior publications undermines claims about reviewer expertise and should be taken into account when assessing review quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard rating form listing explicit evaluation criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a standard rating form in which an explicit set of evaluation criteria is listed for referees to use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A standard form clarifies expectations, promotes consistency, and can be used in training. Editors should explain the relationship between listed manuscript attributes and publishability when using such forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training of referees
rubrics_metrics.description: Train potential referees to increase the quality and reliability of reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training might involve providing samples of actual editorial evaluations and subsequent publication decisions. A collection of reviews and articles on which experts agree (e.g., 'high quality, very publishable; low quality, reject') can be used as training or screening material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author-based reviewer evaluation (author review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors evaluate the reviews they receive (author review) as a mechanism for reviewer accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors would send questionnaires to authors to rate reviews (fairness, carefulness, constructiveness) and keep the returned cards under reviewers' names. Periodic examination of these evaluations could inform editorial decisions about retaining or dismissing reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic monitoring of referee reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematically monitor and evaluate the quality of referee reports by judges, authors, and editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular monitoring should have a corrective effect on review practices; referees with records of unreasonable or idiosyncratic criteria could be identified and managed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open peer commentary / open review system
rubrics_metrics.description: Complement closed peer review with open peer commentary by publishing commentaries and the author's formal response alongside the accepted article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This openness allows readers to examine and appraise the review process and the substantive debate ('creative disagreement') and increases transparency and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blind review (double-blind) to reduce prestige bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Use blind reviews as a policy to minimize the influence of institutional affiliation and author prestige on acceptance decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blind reviewing must be implemented conscientiously; it may not eliminate identification (e.g., via personal citations) and can introduce other problems. Evidence suggests an increase in journals using blind review, but effectiveness should be evaluated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central computer bank of rejected papers/authors to deter 'journal shopping'
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposal to create a central database listing titles and authors of rejected papers, categorized (a) rejected, (b) acceptable but not sufficient/appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distributed to editors (or placed on accessible tapes) to deter repeated resubmission of poor manuscripts. Beware of potential negative halo effects and reputational harm for labeled authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial explanation of attributes-to-publishability relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should explain how specified attributes of submitted manuscripts relate to decisions about publishability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such explanations increase transparency, help referees align judgments with editorial expectations, and can support referee training and consistent editorial decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial selection: novelty/importance vs scientific adequacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Different journals place differing emphasis on criteria such as scientific adequacy (competence) versus novelty/importance (newsworthiness); subjective importance can increase variability and chance in acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize when 'importance' is a subjective criterion (e.g., Physical Review Letters' shift from 'novel and newsworthy' to 'important') and consider community-level mechanisms (open debate) to resolve controversies rather than leaving them solely to referees and editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical and practical constraints when studying peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical studies of the review process (e.g., deceptive resubmissions) entail ethical and practical costs and obstacles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared for lengthy time commitments, difficulties obtaining published materials and editorial cooperation, and objections to the research approach; weigh deception concerns and be ready for editorial and community reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess Type I and Type II error rates in journal acceptance decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the rates of false positives (accepting flawed work) and false negatives (rejecting quality papers) in peer review; existing analyses suggest Type II errors may be substantially higher than Type I.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use citation indices, interrater reliability, and acceptance rates to estimate error types; extreme regression-only explanations would imply unreasonably high Type II error rates, so empirical measurement is necessary.
